item.title: Winfried Schumann and the Resonances of the Earth
item.description:
Winfried Schumann and the Resonances of the Earth
A German physicist does a division: the circumference of the Earth divided by the speed of light. The result — 7.83 hertz — has become the planet's alleged "heartbeat". In 1952, Winfried Otto Schumann, a German electrical engineer, published with his student the demonstration that the Earth and the ionosphere form a resonant cavity. He will never hear his own voice — but his equations are today the instrument that science uses to count the thunderstorms of the world, to track tropical temperature, and to hunt for hydrocarbon deposits off the coasts. This episode tells the story of the man, of the cavity, of the measurements that finally came — and it sorts out physics from the promises of healing: Schumann resonances are a measuring instrument, not a medicine. 🎙️ "Who's That Guy?" — Portraits · Interviews · History ⚠️ This programme is a work of fictional radio biography, of a historical and heritage character. item.title: Beethoven Facing the Silence
item.description:
Beethoven Facing the Silence
Vienna, winter 1826. The greatest composer in the world no longer makes out a single note. In his apartment, questions are written to him in a notebook — and he answers out loud, rough and free. The most famous deaf man who ever lived, brought back to life through an interview he could never actually hear.
How did a man who went completely deaf compose the Ninth Symphony, the Ode to Joy, the last quartets? Through this fictional interview built on real facts, Beethoven tells of the whistling that began at 26, the Heiligenstadt Letter in which he admitted he wanted to die, the piano with its legs removed and the baton held between his teeth so he could feel the vibrations, that evening of 1824 when a singer had to turn him towards the standing audience he could not hear — and of silence becoming, against all expectation, his greatest master.

item.title: Marie Curie — The Woman With Two Nobel Prizes
item.description:
Marie Curie — The Woman With Two Nobel Prizes
What if a discovery could light up the world twice — and cost the woman who made it her life? Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, Marie Curie became the only person ever to receive two Nobel Prizes in two different sciences: physics in 1903, chemistry in 1911.
In this imagined interview, we follow her road: the Polish girl who studied in secret in a "flying university" before boarding the train to the Sorbonne; the meeting with Pierre Curie; the announcement of polonium in July 1898 and radium in December; the terrible years in a dilapidated shed where tons of pitchblende were processed without protection; the first chair ever held by a woman professor at the Sorbonne; the "little Curies" of the First World War; and her daughter Irène, who won a Nobel Prize of her own in 1935. Marie Curie speaks here of her philosophy of work, transmission and perseverance — and of the terrible price paid for a discovery whose danger was still unknown.

item.title: Don Miguel Ruiz — The Four Agreements
item.description:
Don Miguel Ruiz — The Four Agreements A Mexican surgeon falls asleep at the wheel and survives a crash that should have killed him. He walks away from medicine — and writes one of the most widely read spiritual books of all time.
In this documentary portrait, we follow Miguel Ángel Ruiz from his mother's healing house in Guadalajara to the operating room, from the highway accident that changed his life to his return to his family's Toltec tradition. We walk through the four agreements one by one — be impeccable with your word, don't take anything personally, don't make assumptions, always do your best — with a warm but critical eye: who were the real Toltecs of Tula, what the modern "Toltec" revival owes to the twentieth century, and why psychologists still find echoes of cognitive therapy in these four simple sentences.
🎙️ Who's That Guy? — Fictional interviews & documentary portraits with history & science. ⚠️ This program is a documentary portrait for educational and cultural purposes. Our analysis reformulates the four agreements and does not reproduce Don Miguel Ruiz's text, whose rights remain with the author. 📚 Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Miguel_Ruiz · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Four_Agreements · https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toltec #DonMiguelRuiz #TheFourAgreements #Toltec #toltecwisdom #spirituality #personaldevelopment #selfhelp #mindfulness #MexicanHistory #WhoIsThatGuy

item.title: Alfred Tomatis — The Man Who Taught Us to Listen
item.description:
Alfred Tomatis — The Man Who Taught Us to Listen
What if your ear did much more than just hear? What if it powered your brain, your voice, your very energy? French physician Alfred Tomatis spent a lifetime proving exactly that — and his controversial method is still practiced worldwide.
In this episode, we sit down with the inventor of the "Tomatis effect" — the discovery that the voice can only produce what the ear can perceive. From the roar of aircraft factories to the hushed halls of Benedictine monasteries, from Mozart's high frequencies to the filtered voice of a mother heard from the womb, Tomatis reveals how sound shapes us from our very first moments. A conversation about listening, healing, and the three laws that changed our understanding of the human ear.
🎙️ "Who's That Guy?" — Portraits. Interviews. History. ⚠️ This podcast is a work of fiction, but the questions it raises are very real.

item.title: René Quinton — Children of the Sea
item.description:
René Quinton — Children of the Sea
What if your blood was nothing but ancient seawater, preserved in your veins for three billion years? French biologist René Quinton proved exactly that — by draining a dog of all its blood and replacing it with filtered ocean water. The dog lived.
In this episode, we meet the self-taught genius who stunned the scientific establishment, saved thousands of infants from cholera with nothing but seawater, co-founded French aviation, and then vanished from history. From the Academy of Sciences to the maternity wards of Paris, from the Atlantic Ocean to the skies above France, Quinton's story is one of the most extraordinary — and most forgotten — in modern science. A conversation about the sea inside us, the courage to defy the establishment, and the patience of the ocean.

item.title: Quinton Water — Marine Plasma & Its Secrets
item.description:
Quinton Water — Marine Plasma & Its Secrets
Our bodies are walking aquariums. That was René Quinton's great intuition — and from it came one of the most fascinating natural therapies of the 20th century. In this bonus episode, we explore what Quinton Water actually is, where it comes from, and how it is used today.
From the depths of the Atlantic Ocean to pharmacy shelves across Europe, discover the difference between hypertonic and isotonic marine plasma, how to take Quinton ampoules, and why this cold-filtered seawater — rich in every mineral and trace element known to life — is still prescribed by practitioners around the world. A short, practical dive into the ocean inside you.

item.title: 432 vs 440 — The Battle of the Pitch Pipes
item.description:
432 vs 440 — The Battle of the Pitch Pipes
Eight vibrations per second apart, and yet a war without end online: the "universal" tuning fork versus the orchestral standard. A physicist of sound reopens the case and sorts legends from science.
From France's 1859 standard to the Italian decree of 1884 signed for Verdi, from the 1939 London conference to the ISO norm of 1955: the true history of the tuning fork, far stranger than the myth. Then the trial of the legends: 440 imposed by the Nazis? The frequency of water? The Earth's resonance? And above all, what the actual medical studies really say — including the one where anxiety dropped... even without music.
🎙️ "Who's That Guy?" — Episode 1, featuring the return of Doctor Camille Rivière (a fictional character). ⚠️ This program is a work of radio fiction for educational and cultural purposes: the historical and scientific facts are real and verifiable.

item.title: Victor Hugo Facing Misery and Inequality
item.description:
Victor Hugo Facing Misery and Inequality
🎙️ "Who's That Guy?" — Portraits · Interviews · History
This podcast is a work of fictional radio biography with a historical and heritage character. The statements attributed to the character are an imagined reconstruction.
In this ninth episode, Victor Hugo answers questions about the legends that have wrapped around his name for nearly two centuries. From the myth of the pure romantic poet to the reality of the man who wrote from a barricade and a parliamentary bench, this is a conversation with one of the nineteenth century's most formidable voices — conducted entirely in fiction, and grounded in the verifiable record of his life and work.
Hugo corrects the popular image from within: he was not merely the poet of the dispossessed, nor the sentimental romantic, nor the simple man of feeling. He was a novelist, a playwright, a pamphleteer, a politician, and a relentless campaigner for justice. He wrote Les Misérables in 1862 and Notre-Dame de Paris in 1831, opposed Napoleon III and went into exile in Guernsey from 1852 to 1870, and published the famous pamphlet Napoléon le Petit in 1852. The novel he titled Les Misérables, he notes, has never been read by most of its admirers under its own title.

item.title: Martin Luther King Facing Racial Inequality Today
item.description:
Martin Luther King Facing Racial Inequality Today
A fictional radio portrait of Dr. King, revisiting the defining moments of the civil rights movement from the inside. The dialogue is a fictional reconstruction, not a historical recording.
This episode traces King's journey from the "I Have a Dream" speech at the Lincoln Memorial to the Poor People's Campaign, examining nonviolent leadership, the struggle for economic justice, and the unfinished work of racial equality. item.title: Jean-Paul Sartre and the Youth of May 68
item.description:
Jean-Paul Sartre and the Youth of May 68
A philosopher who refused every easy label, a man who stood on barricades and declined the Nobel Prize. Jean-Paul Sartre and the Youth of May 68 revisits the life and myths of one of the twentieth century's most influential thinkers, correcting the caricature from within.
This episode reconstructs a fictional interview with Sartre, in which he addresses the legends that have grown around his name: the radical existentialist, the man of "bad faith," the slogan-monger of "existence precedes essence." He speaks about his major works, from "Nausea" to "Being and Nothingness," about "Existentialism Is a Humanism" and the lecture that changed how millions understand freedom, and about "The Dirty Hands" and the moral ambiguities of political violence. He reflects on his relationship with Simone de Beauvoir and her authorship of "The Second Sex," on founding "Les Temps modernes," on Indochina and the painful contradictions of his own family history, and on May 1968, when the young people of France looked to him as a symbol of committed intellectual life.

item.title: Michel Foucault Facing Youth Violence
item.description:
Michel Foucault Facing Youth Violence
A fictional podcast episode imagining a conversation with Michel Foucault on youth violence in France today. The philosopher corrects misquotations and refuses both to glorify violence and to demonize the young.
This episode traces Foucault's intellectual trajectory from Histoire de la folie (1961) through Surveiller et punir (1975), his years at the Sorbonne and the College de France (1970-1984), and his involvement with the GIPU and the Service d'action ducative. Foucault dismantles the myth of the philosopher who only cared about power, corrects the abusive citation "the prison produces delinquency," and explains how dispositifs, biopower, and governmentality shape the lives of young people.

item.title: Pythagoras — The Music of the Spheres
item.description:
Pythagoras — The Music of the Spheres
A philosopher who heard the universe in numbers — and a legend that grew louder than the man himself.
Step into the imagined world of Pythagoras, the Ionian Greek who united mathematics, music, and the heavens into a single vision of cosmic order. This episode of "Who's That Guy?" presents a fictional interview that separates the attested teachings of the historical Pythagoras — metempsychosis, the tetraktys, the mathematical foundations of harmony — from the myths that later centuries have draped over his name. From the monochord to the music of the spheres, from the school of Croton to the burning of its meeting houses, this is a portrait built from the fragments Aristoxenus and Diogenes Laertius left behind.
The Pythagorean school was not the work of one man but of a community of initiates who pursued knowledge as a path to purification. Their ideas — the sphericity of the Earth, the doctrine of proportions, the link between music and ethics — traveled across centuries and shaped the astronomy of Hipparchus, the cosmology of Copernicus, and the physics of Newton. Yet every attribution must be weighed, every legend questioned. This is not a hagiography. It is a conversation with an echo, asking what we can truly know about the man who said that all is number.

item.title: Simone de Beauvoir — The Philosopher of the Second Sex
item.description:
Simone de Beauvoir — The Philosopher of the Second Sex
A fictional radio portrait of the existentialist philosopher, writer, and feminist activist who wrote The Second Sex and changed the conversation about gender forever.
From a bourgeois Catholic childhood in Paris to the agrégation de philosophie in 1929, from the lifelong partnership with Jean-Paul Sartre to the publication of one of the most controversial books of the twentieth century — this episode traces the arc of a woman who refused to be defined by anyone else's terms.
Simone de Beauvoir was not just a philosopher. She was a novelist, a political activist, an editor of Les Temps Modernes, and a voice for the feminist movement of the 1970s. Her work on the social construction of gender, her analysis of women's oppression across history, and her insistence that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" remain foundational to feminist thought today. This is a fictional reconstruction — not a real interview — brought to you as part of the "Who's That Guy?" portrait series.
